extracted.intended_audience: War Department officials, contracting officers, accounting officers, government attorneys, and surety companies dealing with official and contractor bonds
extracted.subtask_description: Administrative and legal standards governing official bonds (disbursing officers, sureties, partners) and contractor bonds for the War Department: when bonds are required, their form, approval, sufficiency of sureties/amounts, effect of substitutions, filing, and liability rules. Focused on U.S. federal/War Department practice and applicable statutes/regulations of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governing law for official bonds accepted by the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: An official bond, made to the United States, is a contract to be performed at Washington and is to be governed as to its interpretation, obligation, and legal effect by the law of the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bonds given for improvement of Bayou Teche, La., though executed elsewhere, should be accepted in the State where acceptance is to be made; law of the place of acceptance governs formalities of execution (recommendation to refer bonds to district engineer for acceptance where appropriate). C. 2625, Sept. 1, 1909.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department has exclusive duty to take and approve bonds; Treasury cannot review
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of taking and approving bonds under the War Department rests entirely in the War Department; the Treasury Department has no authority to review the action of the War Department or pass upon sufficiency of sureties on such bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority cited: Nov. 2, 1891; Apr. 18, 1908; July 23, 1909; Aug. 6, 1909; U.S. v. Garlinghouse and other authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department practice — bonds not surrendered after due performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after due performance of the conditions of a bond, it is contrary to the practice of the department to surrender such bonds; records will show performance and bondsmen may be advised of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice may be given with caution that information is not intended to compromise U.S. interests if the contract has not in fact been fully performed. C. 18610, Sept. 20, 1907; C. 18589, Sept. 21, 1905.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory obligations (e.g., act Aug. 13, 1894) may prevent surrender of a bond
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statute requires protections (e.g., contractor must promptly pay labor/materials and Secretary must furnish copy of bond to laborers and material-men), such provisions may deprive the Secretary of authority to surrender the bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning bonds refused by United States is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no objection to returning a bond that the United States refused to accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority to cancel or release a bond absent statute
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of statute, no executive officer has authority to cancel or nullify a bond or release a surety thereon; such a release cannot be given even if other sureties of undoubted financial responsibility exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-and-several wording not universally required
rubrics_metrics.description: There being no law requiring bonds under the War Department to be joint and several, a bond worded so that each surety is bound as to a specific part only of the penalty and not jointly and severally may be legally sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23165, Apr. 30, 1908; but see Army Regulations par. 576 (1910) requiring certain official bonds to be joint and several.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partners lack implied authority to execute sealed contracts (bonds) for firm
rubrics_metrics.description: The implied authority of a partner to execute contracts for the firm does not extend to contracts under seal (bonds); when a partner signs a bond for the firm, evidence of express authority from other partners should be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express authority need not be under seal. C. 5066, Sept. 28, 1898 and other cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seal may be disregarded if instrument does not require one
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instrument, although sealed in fact, is of a character that does not require a seal, the presence of the seal may be disregarded and the instrument treated as a simple contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting bond signed by less than all partners under certain form
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract is made with a partnership there is no legal objection to accepting as a bond one signed by less than all partners, provided those who sign sign as individuals (not as partners) and the partnership name is not signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board resolution granting future signing power does not ratify past bond execution
rubrics_metrics.description: A resolution of a board of directors purporting to vest the treasurer with power to make and sign all necessary contracts is prospective only and does not ratify execution of a bond already made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of accepting a substituted bond with lower penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: If a new bond in a lesser penal sum is accepted as a substitute with recitals that it is intended as a substitute and that the old penalty is unnecessarily large, the loss will fall entirely on sureties under the new bond to the extent of its penalty; the U.S. might still sue under the old bond, and new sureties may be liable to old sureties for recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting personal sureties for corporate surety does not release old bond absent provision
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor may present a further bond signed by personal sureties in lieu of a corporate bond to avoid premium payments; but such substitution does not release the old bond unless special provision allows discontinuance — the old bond ordinarily remains in full force for defaults up to the date of the new bond and thereafter liabilities may be joint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect and cautionary guidance described; Cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may require bonds even without express statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there may be no express statutory provision requiring a disbursing officer to give a bond, the Government may require such officers to give one (e.g., Secretary of War may require bond where public property entrusted to individuals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 61, Jan. 28, 1892; forms of official bond and Sec. 1191 discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and effective date of official bond to prevent overlapping liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Form of official bond authorized Dec. 31, 1900 secures fidelity from date of approval of the bond, enabling accounting officers to fix responsibility and prevent overlapping bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 9482, Dec. 28, 1900; practice: date of approval often first day of a month except first bond given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving a new bond with same conditions is cumulative; old sureties not released
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bond conditioned the same way is given and accepted, the new bond is cumulative and makes sureties on both old and new bonds responsible for future transactions; a new bond does not release sureties on the old bond absent express provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised bond form language to limit old-bond liability after new bond approval
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of official bond was changed so the condition would bind the officer 'until a new official bond in his case shall be approved,' intending that the old bond, after approval of a new one, remain only to cover defaults prior to approval of the new bond. Attorney General opinion noted some limits depending on statutory prescription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change authorized Dec. 14, 1895 and later; discussion of Attorney General opinion Oct. 17, 1906 (26 Op. Atty. Gen. 70) and differing administrative interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of bond-approval authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of approving bonds (not prescribed by statute) may be delegated by the Secretary of War to other officers (e.g., commanding general, Philippines Division) and approval by delegated authority is valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and sufficiency when corporate surety is sole surety
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a corporation is surety, filing periodic financial statements pursuant to Army Regulations may suffice to demonstrate sufficiency of surety; a corporate indemnity bond signed only by the surety company (not by the officer) may be a sufficient official bond under Sec. 1191 since statute does not prescribe form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits of justification — aggregate vs. individual sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Although regulations contemplate two or more sureties each justifying separately, practice may waive strict compliance if the aggregate justification equals or exceeds the required amount; however, separate affidavits signed by each surety are proper and required in form (irregularities may be waived).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 4-, 1878; R. 34, 147, Feb. 27, 1873; further citations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each surety's obligation on disbursing officer bond must be for whole penalty when regulation so requires
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation of each surety on a disbursing officer's bond must be for the whole amount of the penalty where regulation requires the sureties to be jointly and severally bound for whole amount; contradictory handwritten amounts under signatures render instrument unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official bond limited to office held — effect of promotion/resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: An official bond limited to the office held at the time of giving becomes inoperative upon promotion or cessation of the office; it remains a valid obligation to cover any defaults between execution and promotion/cessation. If conditioned to run 'until a new official bond in his case is approved', then it will terminate upon approval of the new bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 1999, Jan. 22, 1896; C. 9482, Dec. 21, 1900; related examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond continues in force during non‑disbursing duty if language provides
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bond is to continue in force while the officer holds his office until a new bond is approved, the bond continues in force even if the officer is performing duties not calling for disbursement of money (e.g., detailed on General Staff); it will still secure fidelity upon return to disbursing duties. Agreements exempting premium payments while on non‑disbursing duty do not affect surety liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointment nuance — bond coverage may not extend after confirmation unless provision included
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond given under a recess appointment may not cover fidelity after confirmation by the Senate unless the bond's condition expressly covers both the recess appointment and later commission; otherwise, a new bond is required for the confirmation/commissioned office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers may act as sureties though not favored
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statute or regulation prohibiting an Army officer from acting as surety on the official bond of another officer, but such a relation is not favored in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous recitals in bond do not necessarily invalidate if office sufficiently described
rubrics_metrics.description: An incorrect recital (e.g., stating appointment in 'Army of the United States' when in Volunteer Army) is not inconsistent with fact; the actual office may be shown by parol and the bond may be held valid if other descriptive words sufficiently identify the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's regulation for renewal/substitution of official bonds (Par. 583)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 583 A.R. provides that in case of financial embarrassment or disqualifying cause on part of surety, the Secretary of War will require renewal of the bond; official bonds may not be renewed at will of principal or surety, and substitution of one corporate surety for another is not permitted except by direction of the Secretary or after the bond has run four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: dissatisfaction with a surety company's rate is not sufficient to justify submission of a new bond; C. 25462, Aug. 8, 1910.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing location for bonds relating to insular/military governments
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond to secure faithful disbursement of funds relating to the military government of Cuba should be filed in the Insular Bureau, not in the Treasury Department; bonds covering funds not strictly public should run to appropriate official (e.g., superintendent) in trust and be filed at relevant headquarters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement to examine bonds biennially (act Mar. 2, 1895) — sufficiency of sureties and amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Act of Mar. 2, 1895 requires every officer taking official bonds to cause them to be examined at least once every two years as to sufficiency of sureties and to examine/fix amount at least once in two years or more often as necessary; compliance may be met via prescribed certificates/reporting procedures by bureau chiefs and periodic statements for corporate sureties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Order 29, Adjutant General's Office, May 1, 1895; C. 1414, June 8, 1895; C. 448, Dec. 1, 1896; instructions on reporting lists and recommendations to Secretary of War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability limited to obligor's own duties and supervision — not automatically strict for subordinate acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bond conditions that obligor 'carefully discharge the duties of his office or employment', if a subordinate (not selected/discharged by obligor) receives custody of property, the obligor is required only to discharge his own duties, including supervision, and is not liable for loss resulting from neglect/misconduct of the subordinate if he fully performed his supervisory duties. Similarly, a condition to 'faithfully and honestly account for all public property intrusted to his care or custody' does not make him liable for property never coming into his personal physical possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract bonds for supplies/works are administrative; statute requires bonds for construction/repairs and payment provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving bonds to secure performance of contracts for furnishing supplies or doing work for the War Department is a matter of administrative regulation (not universally statutory). The act of Aug. 13, 1894 (as amended Feb. 24, 1905) directs that bonds be required with formal contracts for construction or repairs of public buildings and works and that such bonds contain a provision that the contractor shall promptly make full payments to persons supplying labor and materials; the Secretary fixes penalty amounts by regulation (par. 577 A.R.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See pars. 577-589 A.R., 1910 and statutory citations.
